title: “TOUCH NOT MY ANOINTED”—THE VERSE ABUSIVE LEADERS DON’T WANT YOU TO UNDERSTAND
paragraphs:
“TOUCH NOT MY ANOINTED”—THE VERSE ABUSIVE LEADERS DON’T WANT YOU TO UNDERSTAND
What if the verse you were taught meant “Never question the man of God” was actually spoken by God to protect vulnerable people from powerful men?
There is a sentence that has silenced wounded Christians for years.
Maybe you heard it after asking why the money was handled that way.
Maybe someone whispered it when a pastor’s behavior started troubling you.
Maybe you heard it after a victim finally spoke.
Maybe you were told it when you asked a question nobody in leadership wanted to answer.
“Be careful.”
“That’s the man of God.”
“Don’t speak against God’s servant.”
And then came the sentence that ended the conversation:
“Touch not My anointed.”
Suddenly, asking for accountability felt like rebellion against God.
Exposing wrongdoing felt like attacking the church.
Questioning a leader felt like questioning Jesus Himself.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility was planted inside your conscience:
What if God punishes me for speaking?
So you became quiet.
But the question remained.
Does the Bible actually teach that spiritual leaders are beyond examination, correction, rebuke, or accountability?
Open the passage.
Not the slogan.
Not the sermon clip.
Not the sentence somebody quoted when uncomfortable questions started being asked.
The passage.
Psalm 105:15 says:
“Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm.”
The same declaration appears in 1 Chronicles 16:22.
And the Hebrew deserves to be seen:
אַל־תִּגְּעוּ בִמְשִׁיחָי וּבִנְבִיאַי אַל־תָּרֵעוּ
’Al-tigge‘u bimshichai, uvinvi’ai ’al-tare‘u.
“Do not touch My anointed ones, and do My prophets no harm.”
Notice something immediately.
The Hebrew translated “My anointed” is בִמְשִׁיחָי — bimshichai.
It is plural.
“My anointed ones.”
That matters.
Because Psalm 105 is not a divine press release granting one modern religious personality immunity from scrutiny.
Read backward.

The psalm is recounting God’s covenant faithfulness to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and their descendants. It remembers a people who were few in number, wandering from nation to nation and kingdom to kingdom.
Then Scripture says that God “suffered no man to do them wrong” and reproved kings for their sake.
Then comes the declaration:
“Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm.”
In other words, the picture is almost the reverse of how the verse can be weaponized today.
The text shows God restraining powerful rulers from harming the people under His covenant care.
It is not a powerful religious ruler telling vulnerable people:
“You cannot question me.”
That distinction is enormous.
And once you see it, you may never hear the verse the same way again.
This does not mean Christians have permission to slander pastors.
It does not mean every accusation is automatically true.
It does not mean church members should become suspicious, rebellious, vindictive, or eager to destroy reputations.
Scripture condemns false witness.
Scripture condemns gossip.
Scripture condemns malicious speech.
And Scripture specifically protects elders against unsupported accusations.
Paul writes in 1 Timothy 5:19:
That protection matters.
A pastor’s reputation should not be destroyed because somebody is angry, offended, jealous, confused, or spreading an allegation without sufficient evidence.
But keep reading.
Because verse 19 does not erase verse 20.
“Them that sin rebuke before all, that others also may fear.”
There it is.
The same Bible that protects an elder from reckless accusations refuses to protect a sinning elder from accountability.
Biblical honor and biblical accountability are not enemies.
They belong together.
And Paul drives the point even deeper in the next verse by warning Timothy to carry these instructions out “without preferring one before another, doing nothing by partiality.”
No favoritism.
Not even when the person involved has a title.
Not even when he can preach.
Not even when thousands follow him.
Not even when his ministry has accomplished genuine good.
Not even when confronting what happened would embarrass the church.
Because Jesus did not die to create celebrity kingdoms where gifted men become untouchable.
He died to purchase a people for Himself.
There is only one Head of the Church.
Jesus Christ.
There is only one name before which every knee will ultimately bow.
Jesus Christ.
There is only one Shepherd who owns the sheep.
Jesus Christ.
Pastors are shepherds only beneath the Chief Shepherd.
That is why Peter tells elders not to exercise leadership by “lording it over” those entrusted to them, but by becoming examples to the flock.
Jesus Himself drew an unmistakable contrast between worldly authority and kingdom leadership. Gentile rulers exercise dominion over people, He said, “but it shall not be so among you.”
Then Christ turned the entire pyramid upside down.
Whoever would become great must become a servant.
Think about that.
Jesus never told His apostles:
“Now that you possess spiritual authority, make sure nobody questions you.”
He washed feet.
The King knelt down.
The Lord wrapped Himself in a towel.
The One who genuinely possessed all authority became the Servant in the room.
So whenever Christian leadership requires intimidation to preserve its authority, something has already moved dangerously far from the basin and towel of Jesus.
And perhaps somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You did not want to destroy your church.
You loved your church.
That was why it hurt.
You did not enjoy discovering something was wrong.
You wished desperately that you were mistaken.
You prayed.
You questioned yourself.
You wondered whether you were being judgmental.
You remembered every sermon about submission.
You remembered Hebrews telling believers to obey their leaders.
You remembered David refusing to kill Saul.
And maybe someone reminded you:
“David would not touch God’s anointed.”
That story deserves context too.
David had opportunities to physically kill Saul.
He refused.
That is beautiful.
David would not murder the king in order to seize the throne God had promised him.
But David’s refusal to kill Saul did not mean David pretended Saul was righteous.
Read the story carefully.
David confronted Saul.
David described Saul’s pursuit of him as wrong.
David fled from Saul.
David did not remain within spear-throwing distance to prove his submission.
That sentence may free somebody.
You can refuse vengeance without pretending abuse is holy.
You can forgive someone without giving them unrestricted access to hurt you again.
You can honor legitimate spiritual authority without surrendering your conscience to another human being.
You can refuse to retaliate and still tell the truth.
David would not murder Saul.
But neither did David hand Saul another spear.
There is a difference between forgiveness and enabling.
Between honor and idolatry.
Between submission and surrendering moral discernment.
Between protecting the unity of Christ’s church and protecting somebody’s image at the expense of Christ’s sheep.
And Scripture is painfully realistic about leaders who love power.
There was a man in the early church named Diotrephes.
John describes him with words every Christian leader should fear:
φιλοπρωτεύων αὐτῶν
philoprōteuōn autōn.
The idea is devastatingly simple.
He loved being first among them.
Diotrephes wanted preeminence.
He rejected legitimate apostolic authority, spoke maliciously, interfered with believers who wanted to receive fellow Christians, and put people out of the church.
And what did the apostle John do?
Did John say:
“Well, Diotrephes is a leader. Touch not God’s anointed”?
No.
John said he would call attention to what Diotrephes was doing.
That is in your New Testament.
The Bible itself publicly records the misconduct of a church leader who loved prominence.
God apparently did not believe exposing abusive spiritual behavior was automatically an attack against His Church.
Sometimes exposing darkness is part of protecting the Church.
But here we must guard against another ditch.
Because wounded people can become cruel people.
Exposure can become revenge.
Accountability can become entertainment.
Discernment can become suspicion.
And righteous anger can slowly become hatred while we continue calling it righteousness.
Jesus will not allow that either.
Christian accountability must still look like Christ.
Truth without love becomes a weapon.
Love without truth becomes complicity.
Jesus gives us both.
Grace and truth.
So this article is not permission to attack pastors.
Please hear that clearly.
Do not use these words to justify gossip.
Do not weaponize fragments of somebody’s story.
Do not make accusations you cannot substantiate.
Do not confuse personality differences with spiritual abuse.
Do not assume that every difficult decision by church leadership is manipulation.
Do not destroy somebody because you heard one side of a complicated situation.
Pastors are human beings too.
Their families bleed too.
False accusations can devastate innocent people.
That is precisely why biblical processes, evidence, witnesses, wisdom, impartiality, and mature judgment matter.
But neither should “grace” become a religious word for hiding what needs to be brought into the light.
Grace does not require lies.
Forgiveness does not require pretending.
Restoration does not require the absence of consequences.
And repentance is not demonstrated merely by saying, “I’m sorry.”
John the Baptist said:
“Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance.”
Real repentance produces fruit.
It stops defending the sin.
It stops blaming the wounded.
It stops controlling the narrative.
It stops demanding immediate restoration to influence.
It becomes willing to tell the truth even when truth costs something.
Because repentance is not reputation management.
Repentance is agreeing with God about our sin and turning toward Him.
And this is where the message stops being merely about “abusive leaders.”
Because it would be easy to read this entire article thinking about somebody else.
Your former pastor.
That famous preacher.
That ministry scandal.
That manipulative leader.
But the Gospel does not allow us to stand safely outside the courtroom pointing at everyone else.
Eventually Jesus turns the light toward us.
Have you manipulated someone?
Have you used Scripture to win an argument rather than reveal Christ?
Have you demanded grace for yourself while demanding judgment for another?
Have you protected your reputation more fiercely than your holiness?
Have you hurt someone and then become angry because they told the truth about being hurt?
Have you confused being respected with being right?
Maybe you never stood behind a pulpit.
Maybe your kingdom is your home.
Your marriage.
Your workplace.
Your Facebook page.
Your reputation.
Your little circle where nobody is allowed to challenge you.
The human heart loves thrones.
That is why all of us need the cross.
The deepest problem in abusive Christianity is not merely bad leadership technique.
It is sin.
And the deepest answer is not merely better organizational policy.
We need Jesus.
The Jesus who confronted hypocritical religious leaders.
The Jesus who welcomed the bruised.
The Jesus who touched lepers.
The Jesus who defended the vulnerable.
The Jesus who told powerful men the truth.
The Jesus who also looked at sinners with astonishing mercy and said, in effect, leave your life of sin.
The Jesus who carried our guilt to Calvary.
There, something infinitely greater than reputation management happened.
The sinless Son of God was treated as condemned so condemned sinners could receive mercy.
He was mocked.
Stripped.
Pierced.
Crucified.
And while human beings were busy protecting kingdoms, Jesus was opening His Kingdom to sinners through His blood.
Then the grave could not keep Him.
Christ rose.
That changes everything.
It means your worst sin does not have to become your final identity if you truly come to Christ in repentance and faith.
It means what somebody did to you does not have to write the final chapter of your life.
It means the leader who genuinely repents is not beyond grace.
It means the wounded believer is not beyond healing.
It means churches devastated by scandal can still discover restoration when truth, repentance, justice, wisdom, and grace are allowed to meet beneath the lordship of Jesus.
This is why our message is not “From Scandal to Cancellation.”
It is From Scandal to Grace.
But biblical grace is expensive.
It cost Jesus blood.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace enters darkness carrying a cross.
Maybe you were wounded by someone who represented God so badly that you began confusing that person with God Himself.
Please hear this.
Jesus is not your abusive pastor.
Jesus is not the manipulative ministry leader who frightened you into silence.
Jesus is not the Christian celebrity who disappointed you.
Do not measure the perfection of Christ by the failures of people who carry His name.
Look at Jesus.
When shepherds fail, look at the Chief Shepherd.
When Christians disappoint you, look at Christ.
When religious hypocrisy makes you want to walk away, remember that Jesus reserved some of His strongest words for religious hypocrisy too.
Do not allow somebody else’s counterfeit Christianity to steal the real Christ from you.
And if you are a pastor, elder, ministry leader, teacher, parent, husband, mentor, or anybody carrying influence, perhaps this message needs to become a prayer rather than an argument:
“Jesus, never let my calling become my idol.”
“Never let my authority become my identity.”
“Never let my platform become more precious than Your people.”
“Never let me quote Scripture to escape the correction Scripture itself gives me.”
And if you have been wounded, perhaps your prayer is simpler:
“Jesus, help me trust You again.”
Maybe tears came before the sentence finished.
He sees them.
But healing does not always mean returning to the place where you were wounded.
Sometimes wisdom requires distance.

Sometimes serious misconduct should be reported to appropriate church authorities or, where crimes or immediate danger are involved, to civil authorities. Romans 13 does not describe governing authorities as meaningless simply because wrongdoing occurred inside a church building.
The Church should never require victims to choose between biblical faithfulness and legitimate protection from criminal harm.
And if somebody told you that reporting a crime is “touching God’s anointed,” they have placed a burden upon that verse that its context does not bear.
God is not glorified by protecting darkness.
He is glorified when His people walk in the light.
So what does “Touch not My anointed” actually teach us?
It teaches us something magnificent about God.
He protects those who belong to Him.
He remembers His covenant.
He sees vulnerable people wandering among powerful kingdoms.
Kings are not beyond His authority.
Human power does not frighten Him.
And nobody becomes God merely because people call him “anointed.”
In fact, Scripture ultimately leads us toward the Anointed One above every anointed servant.
מָשִׁיחַ — Mashiach.
Messiah.
Christos in Greek.
Christ.
Jesus is the Christ—the Anointed One.
The Church belongs to Him.
The pulpit belongs to Him.
The pastor belongs to Him.
The wounded person belongs to Him.
The truth belongs to Him.
That should terrify abusive leaders.
And comfort wounded sheep.
If this exposed something you have been afraid to admit, do not turn the comments into a courtroom and do not name people recklessly. But you can say something about your own heart.
And pastors—if you are reading this with humility rather than defensiveness—perhaps simply comment, “Jesus, keep me accountable.”
Imagine what could happen if Christian comment sections became places of repentance instead of warfare.
Not because every disagreement is abuse, but because sooner or later someone may quote those four famous words without their context, and you may need to remember what Scripture actually says.
And consider sending this privately to the person who is suffering quietly and needs to know that honoring Christ does not require calling evil good.
Stay close to daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered not on personalities, but on Jesus Christ.
It does not.
Not because Christians must financially support this particular ministry to glorify God.
Scripture would not permit us to make that claim.
We glorify God through Christ-centered obedience, love, generosity, truth, worship, holiness, and faithful stewardship.

But if this ministry is genuinely feeding you spiritually and you want to help more people encounter biblical truth, your voluntary support can become one practical expression of generosity toward Gospel work.
And there is something else we want believers to know.
He is the treasure.
He is the Savior.
He is the Shepherd.
He is the King.
And perhaps that is the truth somebody tried to make you forget:
No pastor is your Messiah.
No denomination died for you.
No ministry shed its blood for your sins.
No Christian celebrity walked out of a grave for your justification.
Jesus did.
So honor faithful shepherds.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Support them.
Protect them from malicious accusations.
And when leaders sin, follow Scripture rather than celebrity.
Seek truth without vengeance.
Accountability without hatred.
Justice without self-righteousness.
Restoration where genuine repentance makes restoration appropriate.
Grace without pretending sin never happened.
Because biblical accountability does not threaten the lordship of Jesus.
It proves that we actually believe in it.

And maybe tonight, somewhere behind a locked bedroom door, a wounded Christian will finally realize that the voice saying, “Never question what happened because you’ll be touching God’s anointed,” was not the voice of the Shepherd.
Maybe that person will open a Bible again.
Maybe they will pray again.
Maybe they will walk into a healthy church again.
Maybe they will discover that Jesus was never the One holding the spear.
And maybe a leader reading this will put down his defenses, call the person he wounded, confess without excuses, submit himself to accountability, and discover something scandalously beautiful:
The Gospel has room for repentant leaders too.
Because the cross is not where God teaches us how to protect our image.
The cross is where our image-management dies.
And resurrection is where Jesus begins writing something new.
Remember this when somebody tries to make a human leader too sacred to question:
The safest place for Christ’s sheep is not beneath an untouchable shepherd, but beneath the authority of the Shepherd whose nail-scarred hands proved how far He would go to save them.
